what_it_does: Computer architecture researchers routinely compare designs by reporting 'speedup' — how much faster a new chip is than an old one — and then average those speedups across many test programs using the geometric mean (a common type of average where you multiply numbers and take a root). This paper argues the geometric mean is mathematically wrong for speedup ratios and can actually reverse which design appears better. The authors derive the correct formula from scratch under two explicit scenarios: either both designs run the same amount of work (in which case the harmonic mean — computed by averaging the reciprocals — gives the right answer), or both designs run for the same amount of time (a different harmonic mean formula applies). They back this up with concrete numerical examples showing the geometric and harmonic means can rank competing architectures in opposite order.
